title: Recharge and Lead: Why Smart CEOs Prioritize Sleep and Rest September 17, 2026
author: Heather McGonigal
source: The Human Element, Leadership With a Twist (leadershipwithatwist.substack.com),
summary: In part two of her five-part Coach Heather Fundamentals series on self-care, published with an audio episode but containing a full written piece, Heather McGonigal argues that high performers' ability to push through long days does not make it wise to do so. Her central claim is that rest is not separate from productivity, leadership, or performance but is what fuels sustainable performance, since depleted leaders become less patient, more reactive, less creative, and less flexible even while technically functioning. She widens rest beyond sleep to small restorative pockets such as a walk, music, stretching, or a few minutes without input, and distinguishes these from pseudo-breaks like phone scrolling that pause work without restoring energy. The move of the piece is to make rest personal and observational: leaders should notice what replenishes versus depletes them and treat energy as a limited resource to be managed intentionally. It closes with a concrete invitation to find one pocket of genuine recovery in a typical workday and experiment with how it feels.
points: McGonigal argues that capability for pushing through is not the same as wisdom, and that rest is part of the work rather than a reward for finishing a to-do list.
Depletion shows up in leadership behavior as less patience, magnified small problems, reduced creativity, and more reactive, less flexible responses.
Not every break is restful: twenty minutes of scrolling pauses work without necessarily leaving a person calmer, clearer, or more energized.
The strongest leaders treat energy as a limited resource and are intentional about both spending and restoring it rather than treating themselves like machines.
Her practical assignment is to identify one small pocket of genuine recovery in a typical day, such as ten minutes after a difficult meeting, and then experiment and observe the effect.
quotes: The problem is that being capable of pushing yourself does not mean it is always wise to do so.

When we are depleted, we tend to have less patience. Small problems feel bigger. Creativity gets harder. We can become more reactive and less flexible. We may technically still be functioning, but we are not necessarily operating at our best.
Sometimes rest is ten quiet minutes between meetings instead of filling every available space with another task.
Scrolling through our phones for twenty minutes may give us a pause from work, but it does not necessarily leave us feeling calmer, clearer, or more energized.
The strongest leaders I know do not treat themselves like machines. They understand that energy is a limited resource, and they become intentional about how they use it and how they restore it.
You do not have to earn rest by reaching the end of your to-do list. Most of us would never get there anyway.
The goal is not to build the perfect routine. The aim is to discover what helps you come back to yourself feeling a little more rested, grounded, and ready for what comes next.
